t: Maximum Difference Score in a Grid — Path Minimum DP
o: A path moves down/right arbitrarily far; telescoping shows the total score of any path equals (final cell value) − (minimum cell value along the path, excluding the final cell... including the start). So the best score from paths ending at (i,j) is grid[i][j] minus the minimum grid value among proper predecessors' path-minima. Maintain mn[i][j] = min(grid[i][j], best predecessor min); answer = max over cells of grid[i][j] − min(predecessor minima). Example 1: ending at (2,2)=14 with path-min 5 gives 9. Example 2's best is −1, so we must allow negative answers (initialize to −∞, not 0).
k: Telescoping: path score = last value − minimum value on the path.

a.n: Approach 1: Single-pass DP tracking path minima
a.i: mn[i][j] stores the minimum value on any monotone path ending at (i,j) including itself; the score of the best move into (i,j) is grid[i][j] − min(mn[i-1][j], mn[i][j-1]).
s: Initialize first row/column mn as prefix minima.
For each cell, predMin = min(mn[i-1][j], mn[i][j-1]); update ans with grid[i][j] − predMin; set mn[i][j] = min(grid[i][j], predMin).
a.t: O(m·n) — one DP pass over the grid
a.sp: O(m·n) for the mn table (reducible to O(n) with rolling rows)

a.i: Identical recurrence but keep only the previous row's mn plus the running left value, cutting memory to O(n). Useful follow-up answer for large grids.
s: Keep prevRow[] of path minima and curLeft for the current row.
Overwrite prevRow as the row completes.

w: Biggest trap: initializing the answer to 0 — strictly decreasing grids make the optimum negative (example 2). Second trap: including the cell itself in the predecessor minimum, which fabricates a fake 0-score 'move'. The telescoping identity (score = last − min) is worth stating explicitly in interviews.
